promptText: In the classic double-checked-locking Singleton implementation, why is the `volatile` keyword essential on the instance field?
options: Without volatile, instruction reordering could let another thread observe a non-null reference to a partially-constructed object, since the JVM may publish the reference before the constructor has fully run
volatile is only needed to make the static field visible to instance (non-static) methods
volatile prevents the singleton instance from ever being eligible for garbage collection
volatile is required purely for Java serialization compatibility and has no bearing on thread safety
explanation: The chapter states this directly: without volatile, another thread could see a partially constructed object due to instruction reordering, which is precisely the subtle bug double-checked locking exists to prevent.

promptText: Why is an enum-based Singleton considered the cleanest thread-safe Singleton implementation in Java, ahead of double-checked locking?
options: The JVM guarantees a single instance and handles serialization and reflection attacks for free, with no manual synchronization code required
Enum constants execute on a dedicated background thread separate from the rest of the application
Enum-based singletons cannot be referenced from Spring-managed beans, which the chapter considers a safety feature
Enums eliminate the need for a private constructor, unlike a plain class-based Singleton
explanation: The chapter names `enum Config { INSTANCE; }` as the cleanest option specifically because the JVM itself guarantees a single instance and closes off the serialization and reflection attack vectors that a hand-rolled Singleton must otherwise guard against manually.

promptText: Why does calling an @Transactional-annotated method from within the same class (self-invocation) silently skip the transaction?
options: Spring's default proxy-based AOP (JDK dynamic proxy or CGLIB) only intercepts calls arriving at the proxy from outside the object; a call made directly via `this` inside the same class bypasses the proxy entirely
@Transactional only takes effect on interface methods and is silently ignored on any concrete class method
Self-invocation is detected and blocked at compile time by Spring's annotation processor
@Transactional requires the calling method to also be static in order for the transaction to apply
explanation: The chapter ties this directly to the Proxy pattern: Spring AOP wraps the bean in a proxy, and only calls that go through that proxy get intercepted - an internal `this.method()` call never reaches the proxy, so the transactional advice is skipped.

promptText: What is the key structural difference between Factory Method and Abstract Factory?
options: Factory Method hides the creation of a single product behind one method; Abstract Factory creates whole families of related objects that must work together, such as matching buttons, checkboxes and menus for one UI theme
Abstract Factory can only ever be used for constructing database connections, never UI components
Factory Method requires reflection to function, while Abstract Factory never uses reflection
They are the same pattern; Abstract Factory is simply a deprecated name for Factory Method
explanation: The chapter defines the relationship precisely: Factory Method hides one product's creation, while Abstract Factory goes one level up to produce a coordinated family of related products.

promptText: What specific problem does the Builder pattern solve that a large constructor cannot solve cleanly?
options: The "telescoping constructor" problem, where many optional parameters force either an unreadable giant constructor or numerous overloads, while Builder gives readable, step-by-step construction of an immutable result
Builder is required whenever a class implements more than one interface
Builder eliminates the need for the constructed object to ever expose any getters
Builder can only be generated automatically by Lombok and cannot be hand-written
explanation: The chapter frames Builder specifically as the answer to constructors with many parameters, half of them optional, producing readable, immutable objects instead - real examples include Lombok's @Builder, StringBuilder, and WebClient.builder().

promptText: In the Composite pattern, client code calls `.size()` identically on a FileNode leaf and a Directory branch. What is the entire point of this uniformity?
options: The client never needs an instanceof check to know whether it is holding a leaf or a branch, since both implement the same node interface
Composite requires every leaf node to hold an explicit reference back to its parent Directory
Composite only applies to structures with exactly two levels of nesting, never deeper trees
The Directory class must override equals() and hashCode() before size() can be called on it
explanation: The chapter states this is Composite's entire purpose: treating individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly through one shared interface, so the caller never has to branch on which kind of node it is holding.

promptText: Both Strategy and State wrap interchangeable behavior behind a common interface. What is the precise difference in intent between them?
options: Strategy is chosen by the client and stays fixed for a call; State is switched internally by the object itself as it progresses through its own lifecycle, such as an order moving NEW -> PAID -> SHIPPED
State can only be implemented using an enum, while Strategy is not permitted to use an enum at all
Strategy requires Spring's dependency injection to function; State never requires any injection framework
They are functionally identical patterns that differ only in the name given to the implementing interface
explanation: The chapter's differentiator: Strategy is picked by the caller and stays fixed for a call, whereas State is switched internally by the context itself as it transitions through its own lifecycle - structurally similar, but different in who decides and when it changes.

promptText: Bridge and Adapter both introduce an intermediary object. How does Bridge differ from Adapter in the chapter's explanation?
options: Bridge is designed in up front so two independent dimensions of variation (e.g. shape x renderer) can vary independently without a combinatorial explosion of subclasses; Adapter instead patches an already-existing interface mismatch after the fact
Adapter is classified as a behavioral pattern, while Bridge is classified as a creational pattern
Bridge requires the two separate hierarchies to eventually be merged into a single concrete class
Adapter always produces exactly N x M classes while Bridge always produces exactly N + M classes, regardless of the actual design
explanation: The chapter's JDBC example makes this concrete: Bridge decouples an abstraction (Connection) from its implementation (vendor drivers) by design, avoiding an N x M class explosion, whereas Adapter is reactive - it patches a mismatch that already exists between two incompatible interfaces.

promptText: Spring Data literally names its interfaces *Repository while often behaving DAO-like for simple cases. What is the real, practical distinction the chapter draws between Repository and DAO?
options: Repository speaks in domain/collection terms and can span or aggregate multiple data sources behind one clean method; DAO is tied to persistence/technology concerns around a single data source
DAO can only be used against NoSQL databases, while Repository is restricted to JPA-backed relational databases
Repository requires XML-based bean configuration, while DAO cannot be configured with annotations at all
They are entirely unrelated patterns from different pattern catalogues with no conceptual overlap
explanation: The chapter's precise framing: DAO is about HOW data is accessed, Repository is about how the domain THINKS about its data - the distinction matters most when the domain model doesn't map 1:1 onto tables, which is when a true Repository earns its keep hiding joins and aggregation.

promptText: Beyond "it's more common," why does the chapter recommend constructor injection over field injection as the default?
options: Constructor injection allows final fields, guarantees the object is never left partially wired, and makes unit testing trivial via plain `new` with mocks, whereas field injection hides dependencies from the class's public API and requires a container or reflection even in a unit test
Field injection is strictly faster at application startup because it skips constructor invocation entirely
Constructor injection cannot be combined with the @Autowired annotation under any supported Spring version
Field injection is mandatory once a bean declares more than three collaborating dependencies
explanation: The chapter's table is explicit: constructor injection keeps dependencies mandatory and visible, allows final fields, and is trivially testable with plain `new`, while field injection hides dependencies from the API and needs a container or reflection even in tests.

promptText: Null Object and Optional both aim to avoid returning raw null, but the chapter draws a sharp line between them. What is it?
options: Null Object represents a do-nothing behavior meant to be used as a field/collaborator you can still safely call methods on; Optional represents an absent value meant to be used only as a return type the caller must explicitly unwrap
Optional is designed exclusively for primitive types, while Null Object works only with reference types
Null Object has been deprecated in modern Java in favor of using Optional for every use case
Optional can safely be stored as a mutable class field, while a Null Object implementation cannot
explanation: The chapter's contrast: Null Object is for behavior - an object you keep calling methods on across multiple invocations - while Optional is a return-type-only tool that forces explicit unwrapping via map/orElse/ifPresent; storing Optional in a field is itself called out as a code smell.

promptText: According to the chapter, which design pattern does JPA's persistence context (EntityManager/Session) implement, and why does forgetting @Transactional on a mutating method silently lose the change?
options: It implements the Unit of Work pattern, batching dirty entities and flushing them together at commit; without @Transactional, no transaction boundary exists to trigger that flush, so the tracked change is never actually written
It implements the Observer pattern, and a missing @Transactional simply disables event notifications about the change
It implements the Singleton pattern, and the missing annotation causes a second, conflicting EntityManager instance to be created
It implements the Visitor pattern, and the missing annotation prevents any visitor from being invoked on the entity
explanation: The chapter names this directly: the persistence context tracks dirty entities and defers writes until flush/commit, which is exactly why a change made without an active transaction boundary is silently lost - no flush ever happens.

promptText: The chapter says replacing Visitor with a sealed interface plus an exhaustive pattern-matching switch flips Visitor's classic trade-off. Explain precisely how the trade-off flips.
options: With classic Visitor, adding a new operation is easy (write one new visitor) but adding a new node type is hard (every existing visitor must be updated); with sealed types + exhaustive switch, adding a new operation is still just a new switch method, but adding a new permitted type now makes the compiler flag every non-exhaustive switch across the codebase - turning a silent runtime risk into a compile-time safety net
Sealed types make both adding new operations and adding new types equally difficult, the opposite of Visitor's asymmetry
Sealed interfaces eliminate the need for writing any operation-adding code at all, since methods are generated automatically
The trade-off does not actually change; sealed types are purely syntactic sugar with identical trade-offs to Visitor
explanation: This is exactly the synthesis the chapter draws: Visitor was a workaround for the language lacking a closed, exhaustively-checked union type - sealed types plus pattern matching give the compiler that guarantee directly, so the hard side of the trade-off moves from 'update every visitor silently' to 'the compiler forces you to handle every case.'

promptText: A team needs each customer to configure their own retry/caching policy at runtime based on subscription tier, then apply it around a shared downstream call. Why does the chapter say a straightforward Spring AOP pointcut is the wrong tool here, and what combination does it recommend instead?
options: AOP pointcuts are normally static, matched by class/method and decided at proxy-creation time, so they can't vary per customer at runtime; the fix is a Strategy object for the swappable policy itself, selected per request, wrapped in a Decorator/Proxy that applies whichever policy was selected for that customer
AOP pointcuts already vary per customer natively via a built-in runtime tenant-ID parameter, requiring no additional pattern
The correct fix is to hand-write 20 separate @Around advices, one hardcoded per customer subscription tier
This requirement can only be solved by disabling Spring AOP entirely and writing manual try/catch blocks in every service method
explanation: The chapter's deciding detail: AOP pointcuts are matched and fixed at proxy-creation time, not per-request, so per-customer runtime variation needs an injected or looked-up Strategy object, with the Decorator/Proxy layer applying whichever policy is currently selected.

promptText: The chapter draws a line between GoF class-level design patterns and architecture-level distributed patterns (Circuit Breaker, Saga, CQRS, API Gateway). Why does calling Circuit Breaker "a GoF pattern" signal shallow preparation?
options: GoF patterns organize how objects collaborate within a single process; Circuit Breaker, Saga and CQRS instead coordinate state and failure across independent services over a network - a different class of problem belonging to distributed-systems/microservices design, not the 1994 Gang of Four catalogue
Circuit Breaker actually is one of the original 23 GoF patterns, so the premise of the question is incorrect
GoF patterns were designed exclusively for distributed systems, which makes the distinction the chapter draws meaningless
Architecture-level patterns are simply newer marketing names for Proxy and Decorator, with no material difference between them
explanation: The chapter states this explicitly as a seniority signal: GoF patterns organize code within a process; Circuit Breaker/Saga/CQRS solve a fundamentally different problem - coordinating state and failure across a network - which belongs to the Microservices/System Design chapters, not this one.
